title: We Don't Overcomplicate Things Because They're Hard

conversation.headline: The flinch before the fear
paragraphs: Episode 4 with Moishy Klein hit on something I haven't been able to shake: we don't avoid things because they're complex. We call them complex so we have an excuse not to start.

I know this pattern well. I spent months trying to "figure out" Facebook before I ever posted anything. Not the algorithm — just Facebook. People posting updates about their lives. There was nothing to figure out. But complexity gave me cover.

What I've come to realize is that this isn't really a confidence problem. It's a reflex. The brain flags something as hard, you flinch — and the flinch happens before your self-belief even gets a chance to kick in. Every time I've actually leaned into something I was avoiding — insurance, sales, the theory of evolution — it turned out to be simpler than I'd built it up to be.

paragraphs.quote: The complexity isn't the barrier. The complexity is the excuse. It protects you from having to find out whether you're capable.

paragraphs: The antidote isn't confidence. It's catching yourself mid-flinch and choosing curiosity over avoidance.
conversation.takeaway: Next time something feels too complex to start, ask yourself: is this actually complicated — or am I using complexity as an excuse? Lean in before the flinch wins.

build.headline: I convinced a client to sign. It cost me the client.
paragraphs: There's someone I've known for a long time — someone I looked up to. When the opportunity came to bring them on as a bookkeeping client, I jumped. I was excited. Maybe a little too excited.

I went straight into sales mode. The excitement rushed me through the process — I never took the time to properly understand his situation. Had I slowed down, I would have discovered it quickly: he didn't have a reliable system to track inventory, which meant there was a ceiling on what we could actually do for him.
A month later, he was gone. And in his words — it hurt every time a payment came out of his bank account, because he wasn't getting what he needed.

That one landed. I let my excitement override my judgment. I sold him something before I understood what winning looked like for him. If I'd slowed down, I would've told him from the start: we can't take you where you need to go until your inventory system is sorted. Let's start there.
He might have walked. Or he might have appreciated the honesty and come back ready. Either way, it would've been the right call.
build.takeaway: Before moving to solutions, understand the client's current situation fully. If your service can't deliver what they need right now — say so. A lost deal upfront beats a lost client a month in.

thinking.headline: You can't skip human nature
paragraphs: We have a good side and a dark side. A selfish side and a selfless side. Yin and yang. This isn't a belief — it's a law. You didn't write the software, so you don't get to decide how humans operate.
Most businesses try to ignore this. They treat people like robots and wonder why they have high turnover, unhappy customers, or partnerships that fall apart five years in.

Business done right requires you to lean into both sides at once. The deal that only works for you isn't a deal — it's a time bomb. The partnership where one person wants to make a million dollars and the other wants to work 15 hours a week will hold together until there's real money on the table. Then it fractures.

paragraphs.quote: Know the other person's win before deciding if it's a win for you.

paragraphs: That's not idealism. That's just how sustainable business works. When both sides are winning, the relationship holds. When only one side is — it's only a matter of time.
thinking.takeaway: Before your next deal, hire, or partnership — slow down and get clear on what the other person actually needs to win. Not what you assume. Ask.
